messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Issue with examples of lm.rrpp (package RRPP)
messages.body_plain:
Dear Lucía (and everyone),

I have updated RRPP on Github, version 2.0.1, which was the version it was on Github already but not yet submitted to CRAN.  I was in the process of preparing version 2.0.1 for CRAN when this issue was brought to light, while R updated to version 4.4.0, and while various package-publishing tools also updated.  Because the solution to fix the predict.lm.rrpp bugs was a fundamentally changed coding philosophy, I still need to do some more testing and I also have some other updates to make with regard to the new system of checks performed by CRAN.  However, the functional updates on Github include all I wish to make for version 2.0.1 to submit to CRAN (where version 2.0.0 is most current).

It you install via github, e.g.,

devtools::install_github(“mlcollyer/RRPP”, build_vignettes = TRUE)

the issue should be fixed now.

Please be aware (everyone) that the update by CRAN to version 4.4.0 might mean a bumpy ride for the summer for a lot of packages.  From what I can see, the system for package compliance is changing quite a bit, once again.  Making sure bugs are fixed fast on Github versions of RRPP and geomorph is the best way we can endure the transition.

Best,
Mike

> > Dear Lucía,
> >
> > Thanks for the alert.  This is indeed a bug and not a conceptual difference that should exist.  The clue that demonstrates a problem (with the former example) is that the two PCs for the plot sum to 100% when it should take 3 PCs to explain 100% of the variation (since there are 4 means and 4-1 = 3).  The second example can be trusted.  In performing the analysis “by hand” (running the script step by step) I have isolated that the problem is in the creation of the model design matrix to calculate least-squares means.  A redundancy is introduced that produces a column with all values the same.  When I override this, the model design matrix is the same as in the second example, which means the results converge.
> >
> > How this redundancy came to be I am not yet sure.  I will have to find a new solution, and it might take some time.  In the interim, if you need results, please be aware that the single-factor solution works.  The reason it is not an issue is that full model residuals are bootstrapped to make confidence intervals, and the residuals are the exact same with either approach.  The bug is in the estimation of coefficients with an erroneous model design matrix, which is triggered by the multiple factors.
> >
> > Silent mutations are the worst for coding (bugs that introduce errors do not produce erroneous results).  This slipped past my radar.  I can fix it now that I know the issue exists, so I appreciate the alert.
> >
> > Best wishes,

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Resamplig curves
messages.body_plain:
Bruno,

The sliding of semilandmarks means that during the GPA superimposition, their locations move along the curve or surface such that the bending energy or Procrustes distance between that specimen and the reference is minimized. For curve points, they slide between other points that the user specifies (e.g., landmark 3 slides between 2 & 4).

Resampling is a general statistical process of obtaining values from a set of values. In the case of resampling points along a curve, the curve is specified, and one chooses how many semilandmarks points along it are used to represent that curve. This is a pre-processing step that occurs before GPA. If one is reading shape files digitized from StereoMorph, the ‘readland.shapes’ function allows you to specify how many points are used for each curve.

Finally, I had a quick look at your csv file. I do not know how that was generated but it contains quite a few landmarks with identical coordinates. Those should not be used, as they are redundant.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
If you have the 3D model in a standard format (e.g, obj/ply), you can give  curve resampling in 3D Slicer a try. See https://github.com/SlicerMorph/Tutorials/tree/main/Markups_2
This can give you some idea about whether you have issues with your model.

I don't know how Stratovan does it, but in 3D Slicer if you have missing vertices along the path of the curve, and you force the points to be constrained by the model's surface, and finally you are sampling very densely, some semiLMs may get pushed to the same vertex (since that's the closest one they can be projected on) and hence end up having same coordinate.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Sliding semilandmarks
messages.body_plain:
Bruno,

The short answer is no. The algorithm cannot determine which landmarks are fixed points and which points are semilandmarks without the user providing it some information about that. Without some sort of additional information, it is too much to expect the GPA to just know which landmarks the user intends to use as fixed points and which to use as sliders. That information is user- and dataset-specific.

For semilandmarks on surfaces, one just gives it a list of landmarks that are surface sliders (e.g.,. c(3,4,5,6,…)). That is easy to generate.

For semilandmarks on curves, one must create the slider matrix that you showed in your email. One can attempt to do this with the ‘define.sliders’ function, which allows you to click on the before, slider, after points to generate the matrix. Some users have found this function to be helpful (be sure to read the instructions!).

Dean

Dear Julio,

I think Dean did mean either prep.lda for the RRPP library or predict.lda for the MASS library.  The predict.lda function does exist, but in the MASS library.  The prep.lda function merely prepares either an lm.rrpp or procD.lm fit to use with the lda function (you do not need to use lm.rrpp in place of procD.lm — either works fine).  Once the lda function is used, then the help files for the MASS library should be consulted for options for functions to use with lda objects.

In consulting the help file for the lda function, it is pointed out that an lda object is created only if CV = FALSE, otherwise a list is created.  You can only use the predict.lda function on an lda object; if CV = TRUE, the result is not an lda object.

Whether this is logical, uninformative, confusing, or a mistake, it is unfortunately the domain of the authors of the MASS library  (whom you might contact to inquire why predict.lda cannot be used if CV = TRUE).  Alternatively, realize that your two options to not compete with each other.  The first could be used to calculate discriminant scores; the latter could be used to get a classification table based on cross-validated (jackknifed) posterior probabilities.  If CV= FALSE, there will be a tendency for groups to appear more distinct that they might be because the same data are used to train the model and estimate posterior probabilities — this is considered a circular reasoning problem.  In other words, do not make a table if CV = FALSE but feel free to use this option to get scores.  I think the reason you cannot get scores if CV = TRUE is because rather than one set of vectors, there are n sets of vectors for the n times a single subject is left out.  So there is not a unique set of scores.  This could maybe be better explained with an error statement, but it makes sense why this is a dead-end.

Best,
Mike

Julio,

Just one word of caution.  The posterior probabilities should be more informative than a classification table made from them.  The issue with classification tables is that they make binary decisions based on potentially ambiguous information.  For example, let’s say that a subject from group A could classified as A, B, or C, and the posterior probabilities are:

A B C
0.34 0.33 0.33

This subject would be correctly classified but can one be confident its classification is good?  Alternatively, what if a second subject had the following posterior probabilities?

A B C
0.47 0.48 0.05

This subject would be misclassified as group B even though the probability it is from group A is stronger than the previous subject.  These results (along with others) might demonstrate that groups A and B are similar, even if both are distinct from C, but there might be some subjects that simply cannot be easily classified.

Something like box plots or violin plots of posterior probabilities might be helpful in addition to or in place of classification tables, since they do not require forcing the results into binary variables.

Best,
Mike

messages.subject: problem with function morphol.disparity
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have some scripts using the function "morphol.disparity" and they were working fine. Now, I updated the R package to version 4.4.1, and also the RStudio and the geomorph package to the latest versions. However, the function "morphol.disparity" is now not working properly.
I ran the script below, which is an example from this function in the geomorph manual from March 2024 and the same error message appeared: "error in h(simpleError(msg, call)): error evaluating argument 'a' when selecting method for function 'solve': 'argument is not a QR decomposition' ".
Here is the script:
### Morphol.disparity can be used with previously-defined
### procD.lm or lm.rrpp class objects
data(plethspecies)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land) #GPA-alignment
gp.end <- factor(c(0,0,1,0,0,1,1,0,0)) #endangered species vs. rest
names(gp.end) <- plethspecies$phy$tip
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, phy = plethspecies$phy,
                           gp.end = gp.end)
pleth.ols <- procD.lm(coords ~ Csize + gp.end,
                      data = gdf) # ordinary least squares
pleth.pgls <- procD.pgls(coords ~ Csize + gp.end, phy = phy,
                         data = gdf) # phylogenetic generalized least squares
summary(pleth.ols)
summary(pleth.pgls)
morphol.disparity(f1 = pleth.ols, groups = ~ gp.end, data = gdf,
                  print.progress = FALSE)
morphol.disparity(f1 = pleth.pgls, groups = ~ gp.end,
                  transform = FALSE, data = gdf,
                  print.progress = FALSE) # disparity in tangent space
morphol.disparity(f1 = pleth.pgls, groups = ~ gp.end,
                  transform = TRUE, data = gdf,
                  print.progress = FALSE) # disparity in transformed space

Does anyone know what could be happening?
Thank you very much for your attention.
Sincerely,

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Dear Daniel,

This error is due to recent updates to the RRPP package that cause errors in geomorph.  Because updates to R over the last few years have made it impossible to run examples as part of a CRAN check (why each function has [## Not run:] at the beginning), and because geomorph does not have a function test environment associated with CRAN checks, these sort of errors are not visible until someone stumbles upon them.

You could try adding "verbose = TRUE” as an argument to your pleth.ols and pleth.pgls fits.  I don’t know if this will alleviate the error, but it appears that the error is caused by missing components that now require verbose = TRUE to be included, or have to be added via the function.  It might work, it might not.

Otherwise, you will have to be patient for a bit until geomorph is updated to work with RRPP updates.

Best,
Mike

messages.subject: updates to geomorph and RRPP
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

We wish to alert you about important updates to geomorph and RRPP.  We have submitted new package versions to CRAN (geomorph 4.0.8 and RRPP 2.0.3), which are already available on Github.  (It might take a few days before packages are fully available on CRAN, so installing packages via Github is a good idea.)  These new package versions require R >= 4.4.0, which could mean that you will need to update your version of R to install the packages.  We also recommend this because one of the package dependencies (Matrix) also requires R >= 4.4.0, and we have found that an older version of this package can produce bad results with some geomorph and RRPP functions, rather than errors.  Therefore, we recommend assuring that your package version of Matrix is 1.7.0, along with updating R.

There are no functional changes associated with these updates.  These updates merely accommodate the R and Matrix updates, and improve computational proficiency for RRPP analyses.  There is one new function in the RRPP package (QRforX), which is intended for internal use (to guarantee consistency despite differences in QR decompositions made for dense and sparse model design matrices).  This should improve some analyses (especially using bilat.symmetry or gm.measurement.error) by taking advantage of sparse-matrix algebra.

You can install new packages from Github with the devtools library via:

devtools::install_github("mlcollyer/RRPP", build_vignettes = TRUE)

devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph", ref = “Stable”, build_vignettes = TRUE)

There might be some advantage to using the R package, pak, e.g.,

pak::pkg_install("mlcollyer/RRPP”,…)

where … means “other arguments”.  The pak library might be able to figure out all other packages that need to be updated, whether from CRAN or Github repositories.  However, it might not automatically install vignettes.

Best wishes!

Dean and the geomorph Team

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

messages.subject: post hoc pairwise phylogenetic comparisons
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I performed an ANOVA from OLS (function procD.lm) and also a PGLS (procD.pgls) with the same database and in both cases I got a significant result for shape variation among groups with distinct habitat use. Subsequently, I chose the most appropriate model from PGLS results (in this case a "fit.common") and performed paired comparisons (function pairwise) between the groups to find out which one actually differed from each other. However, researching on the application of these analysis, I recovered a discussion in this group (back in 2016):  https://groups.google.com/g/geomorph-r-package/c/wLLhEgjEPrE?pli=1
stating that, in that time, there was no function in Geomorph to do this for phylogenetic data because the statistical properties of phylogenetic comparative methods applied to pairwise tests were not evaluated. As far as I could search, I could not find any updates on this, including the manuals of recent versions of RRPP and Geomorph packages or some published work. Based on this, I followed Adam's suggestion in that 2016 discussion and performed paired comparisons using the proper model of the ANOVA from OLS and compared it with the results of PGLS paired comparisons. The significant ANOVA from PGLS recovered non significant paired comparisons FOR ALL "test.types" ("dist", "VC", "DL"), which is strange to me since PGLS was significant for habitat use. On the other hand, the significant ANOVA from OLS led to up to 3 out of 6 significant pairwise comparisons depending on the "test.type".
Sorry for the huge text, but I would like to know if: (1) is there any methodological approach to lead with these questions that I missed? (2) if my approach is correct, should I consider the results of OLS or PGLS paired comparisons?
I would really appreciate it if anyone could help me with these issues.
Sincerely,

Daniel

Dear Daniel,

Wow, 8 years passes so fast!  Yes, functions have been updated and yes, you can use pairwise with a PGLS fit.  There is nothing wrong with doing this.  But to answer the other question, no, I do not think theoretical advances have been made in the area of pairwise comparisons for GLS models.  The reason why this is challenging, but isn’t for OLS models, is that although it is easy to make predictions with a GLS model (estimate GLS means), and compare those means, it is not possible to do this with a good sampling distribution with respect to appropriate standard error of the estimates.

Hope fully I can explain this.  The residual covariance for any linear model can be calculated as V = R^T C^-1 R, where ^t means matrix transpose, ^-1 means matrix inverse, R is the matrix of residuals, and C is the matrix of phylogenetic covariances.  R is found from GLS estimation.  C is a N x N matrix for N species.  But if we let C = I, an identity matrix (independence), R becomes OLS residuals instead of GLS residuals.  Algebra still works the same.  We can estimate the standard error of the model fit from V.  However, if we make estimates for g groups rather than N species, there is no way to include C in the calculation, because g != N.  This is of little concern for OLS estimation, because a g x g identity matrix can be used instead of an N x N identity matrix.

With pairwise comparisons, the RRPP distribution of pairwise mean differences is consistent with the distribution of F statistics in ANOVA.  I can show this below.  Notice the bolded P-values.

> library(phytools)
> library(RRPP)
> tree <- pbtree(n= 20)
> y <- fastBM(tree)
> g <- factor(rep(1:2, each = 10))
> names(g) <- names(y)
> y[1:10] <- y[1:10] + 2
> fit.ols <- lm.rrpp(y ~ g)
> fit.gls <- lm.rrpp(y ~ g, Cov = vcv(tree))
>
> pw.ols <- pairwise(fit.ols, groups = g)
> pw.gls <- pairwise(fit.gls, groups = g)
>
> anova(fit.ols)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization

Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I

g          1  9.3241 9.3241 0.31269 8.1891 2.0588  0.016 *
Residuals 18 20.4948 1.1386 0.68731
Total     19 29.8190
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

> summary(pw.ols)

1:2 1.365587  1.148485 1.957779  0.016

The P-values are exactly the same when performing pairwise comparisons between the only two groups as with performing ANOVA.  But if we do the same thing with the PGLS model fit:

> anova(fit.gls)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Generalized Least-Squares (via OLS projection)
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df     SS     MS  Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)
g          1  5.104 5.1040 0.19 4.2223 1.6193  0.045 *
Residuals 18 21.759 1.2088 0.81
Total     19 26.863
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: lm.rrpp(f1 = y ~ g, Cov = vcv(tree))
> summary(pw.gls)

Pairwise comparisons

Groups: 1 2

RRPP: 1000 permutations

LS means:
Vectors hidden (use show.vectors = TRUE to view)

Pairwise distances between means, plus statistics
          d UCL (95%)        Z Pr > d
1:2 1.57239  1.964684 1.202466  0.117

Why did this happen?  There is no apparent way to transform the distances by the phylogenetic covariance matrix, C, for the two estimates made.  The distance between PGLS estimates is not significant even though the between-group variance is.  In ANOVA, variances are appropriate because the residual covariance matrix is the GLS covariance matrix.  In pairwise comparisons, not as much.

I believe the solution is probably to use instead of d, the statistic d/se, where se is the estimated standard error in every random permutation.  This would accomplish the same thing, in principle, as a parametric t-test.  Chances are the standard error would tend to be higher in random permutations in the above example, so the observed d would be relatively larger, if divided by se.

This is the research that still has to be done: find a procedure that produces consistent distributions, despite the inability to properly transform statistics.  If the example above were real data and I found conflicting results, I would interpret the results as the effect of group was slightly significant but evidence was lacking to suggest their means are distinct.  In other words, i would not have sufficient statistical power to detect a meaningful difference between means.

Hope that helps!
Mike

> On Jun 28, 2024, at 3:42 PM, Daniel Fernandes da Silva <danfe...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Dear all,
>
> I performed an ANOVA from OLS (function procD.lm) and also a PGLS (procD.pgls) with the same database and in both cases I got a significant result for shape variation among groups with distinct habitat use. Subsequently, I chose the most appropriate model from PGLS results (in this case a "fit.common") and performed paired comparisons (function pairwise) between the groups to find out which one actually differed from each other. However, researching on the application of these analysis, I recovered a discussion in this group (back in 2016):  https://groups.google.com/g/geomorph-r-package/c/wLLhEgjEPrE?pli=1
> stating that, in that time, there was no function in Geomorph to do this for phylogenetic data because the statistical properties of phylogenetic comparative methods applied to pairwise tests were not evaluated. As far as I could search, I could not find any updates on this, including the manuals of recent versions of RRPP and Geomorph packages or some published work. Based on this, I followed Adam's suggestion in that 2016 discussion and performed paired comparisons using the proper model of the ANOVA from OLS and compared it with the results of PGLS paired comparisons. The significant ANOVA from PGLS recovered non significant paired comparisons FOR ALL "test.types" ("dist", "VC", "DL"), which is strange to me since PGLS was significant for habitat use. On the other hand, the significant ANOVA from OLS led to up to 3 out of 6 significant pairwise comparisons depending on the "test.type".
> Sorry for the huge text, but I would like to know if: (1) is there any methodological approach to lead with these questions that I missed? (2) if my approach is correct, should I consider the results of OLS or PGLS paired comparisons?
> I would really appreciate it if anyone could help me with these issues.
> Sincerely,
>
> Daniel
